\subsection{A second downstream task: POPE}
\label{app:pope}

The downstream check is repeated on a second, independent task: POPE (Li et al.,
arXiv:2305.10355), config \texttt{Full}, split \texttt{random}, revision \texttt{4db12766},
$n=3000$ held-out questions, an object-hallucination probe whose label space is exactly the yes/no
subset that the VQA-RAD check already scores. The \texttt{r5\_step}/\texttt{r6\_step} adapters are
reused unchanged (their \texttt{adapter\_model.safetensors} hashes match the archived VQA-RAD round),
with the same prompt prefix, the same greedy decoding, and the \texttt{norm()}/\texttt{token\_f1()}
definitions imported from that check, so no new answer-parsing rule enters the comparison. All three
arms answer the same $3000$ questions in the same order (the reference arrays are byte-identical across
the three archives). The equivalence margin of $0.05$ is pre-declared and carried over unchanged from
the 451-question analysis; at $3000$ questions the binomial standard error of accuracy is about
$0.0091$, so this set is not at its resolution limit and the margin is not re-fitted.
Table~\ref{tab:pope} reports the arms.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
arm & $n$ & accuracy & token F1 & yes-class F1 & yes rate \\
\midrule
base & 3000 & 0.6257 & 0.6826 & 0.8849 & 0.4327 \\
$r=5$ (per-step) & 3000 & 0.8717 & 0.8717 & 0.8593 & 0.4123 \\
$r=6$ (per-step) & 3000 & 0.8397 & 0.8410 & 0.8237 & 0.3733 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{POPE second downstream task (real images, all 3000 questions, paired by question across arms;
the gold yes rate is exactly $0.5$). The adapters improve exact-match accuracy and token F1 but move
the yes/no prior, and the yes-class F1 therefore moves the other way at $r=6$. Source:
\texttt{tools/\_p1640\_p3\_second\_downstream.py} $\to$
\texttt{outputs/analysis/p3\_second\_downstream.json} (\texttt{arms.*.accuracy},
\texttt{arms.*.token\_f1}, \texttt{arms.*.pope\_f1}, \texttt{arms.*.yes\_ratio}; dataset and protocol
fields in \texttt{meta.dataset} and \texttt{meta.declared\_margins}; confusion counts in the per-arm
archives \texttt{outputs/analysis/p3\_second\_downstream\_\{base,5,6\}.json}).}
\label{tab:pope}
\end{table}

The two adapters are clearly better than the base model on exact-match accuracy (base minus $r=5$:
$-0.2460$, 95\% CI $[-0.2627,-0.2297]$; base minus $r=6$: $-0.2140$, 95\% CI $[-0.2310,-0.1970]$) and on token F1 (base minus
$r=5$: $-0.1891$, 95\% CI $[-0.2030,-0.1752]$; base minus $r=6$: $-0.1583$, 95\% CI $[-0.1731,-0.1438]$); those differences lie
far outside the pre-declared margin, so they are resolved differences rather than equivalences.
POPE's own yes-class F1 moves the other way: base minus $r=5$ is $+0.0256$ (95\% CI $[+0.0152,+0.0364]$), inside the
$0.05$ margin and declared equivalent, whereas base minus $r=6$ is $+0.0613$ (95\% CI $[+0.0481,+0.0747]$), beyond
the margin and not declared equivalent. The mechanism is a shift of the yes/no prior: on a set whose
gold yes rate is exactly $0.5$, the predicted-yes rate falls from $0.4327$ (base) to $0.4123$ ($r=5$) and
$0.3733$ ($r=6$), the false negatives on the $1500$ yes questions rise from $262$ to $324$ and $421$, and the
false positives fall from $60$ to $61$ and $41$. The ranking of the two adapters is consistent across
all three metrics, with $r=5$ better than $r=6$ on accuracy ($+0.0320$, 95\% CI $[+0.0230,+0.0413]$), on token F1
($+0.0307$, 95\% CI $[+0.0218,+0.0398]$) and on yes-class F1 ($+0.0357$, 95\% CI $[+0.0251,+0.0465]$).
\textbf{Boundary.} The downstream effect is therefore \emph{metric-dependent}: both adapters improve
answer accuracy and token overlap, but at $r=6$ the yes/no prior shifts far enough that the balanced
yes-class F1 that POPE measures also degrades beyond the pre-declared margin, while at $r=5$ that F1
stays equivalent to the base model. We make no claim that a downstream accuracy gain certifies the
alignment-energy ordering; what the second task supports is the weaker and more specific statement
that the $r=5$ adapter is the better of the two on all three POPE metrics, the same direction as its
smaller alignment damage. Source: \texttt{tools/\_p1640\_p3\_second\_downstream.py} $\to$
\texttt{outputs/analysis/p3\_second\_downstream.json}
(\texttt{contrasts.base\_minus\_5.*}, \texttt{contrasts.base\_minus\_6.*},
\texttt{contrasts.5\_minus\_6.*}, \texttt{claim\_verdict.metric\_directions}), with the confusion
counts from the per-arm archives.
